title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
study_design: Continuing education overview of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) for healthcare professionals.
clinical_background: PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in females of reproductive age worldwide, with a reported prevalence between 5% and 26% depending on the diagnostic criteria used. Diagnosis generally requires at least 2 of 3 features—chronic ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries—after excluding conditions with similar presentations. Insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, and hormonal dysregulation contribute to its multifactorial pathophysiology. Associated conditions include infertility, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes mellitus, depression, obstructive sleep apnea, endometrial cancer, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Diagnostic delays may allow comorbidities to progress and make lifestyle intervention more difficult.
objectives: Examine diagnostic challenges and the multifactorial pathophysiology of PCOS, including the roles of insulin resistance and hormonal abnormalities.
Recognize why timely diagnosis of PCOS is needed.
Screen patients with PCOS for associated conditions.
Implement appropriate management for patients with PCOS.
Use interprofessional team strategies to improve care coordination and outcomes for patients with PCOS.
main_conclusion: PCOS requires timely, individualized care that addresses reproductive symptoms, metabolic risks, and psychological health. The article emphasizes lifestyle intervention and coordinated care across healthcare professions to improve outcomes and quality of life.
narrative_summary:
This educational review examines the diagnosis, mechanisms, complications, and management of PCOS rather than reporting an original clinical study. It describes a condition affecting between 5% and 26% of reproductive-aged females, with prevalence varying by diagnostic criteria. In adults, diagnosis requires 2 of 3 features—hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian findings on ultrasound or elevated AMH—after conditions with similar presentations are excluded. Adolescents require both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction; ultrasound and AMH testing are not recommended for diagnosis in this group. Insulin resistance, androgen excess, and ovarian hormonal dysregulation are central to the article’s account of pathophysiology.

The review identifies lifestyle modification as the principal management approach and notes that weight loss of about 5% may restore fertility. Combined hormonal contraceptives are first-line treatment for symptomatic menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, and acne, while letrozole is first-line therapy for infertility. It also recommends assessment for associated metabolic and psychological conditions. Screening at diagnosis includes blood pressure, diabetes, and lipids; the article favors a 75 g OGTT over HbA1c for glucose assessment and recommends repeat screening every 3 to 4 years. Because PCOS has reproductive, metabolic, and mental health implications, the review advocates individualized treatment and interprofessional follow-up.
interpretation: PCOS is presented as a lifelong, heterogeneous condition with reproductive and metabolic consequences. Insulin resistance and androgen excess interact in its pathophysiology, while clinical presentation and diagnostic prevalence vary with the criteria applied. Delayed diagnosis may allow associated conditions to progress. Lifestyle changes and modest weight loss can improve symptoms and fertility, but management needs to reflect each patient's reproductive, metabolic, and personal goals. Although risks of several conditions are elevated, the article notes that a prospective study did not find evidence of increased all-cause or cardiovascular mortality.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The article contrasts diagnostic frameworks: Rotterdam Criteria include a broader population than National Institute of Health 1990 Criteria, while RCAES is described as more sensitive than RC for a phenotype involving PCOM and infertility. It reports that RC-defined patients had less prevalent IR than patients identified through NIH or RCAES criteria. Evidence on long-term outcomes is mixed: a retrospective Western Australian cohort reported more hospital admissions and several diagnoses among women with PCOS than in the general population, whereas a 32-year prospective study found no evidence of increased all-cause or cardiovascular mortality. The treatment discussion cites studies favoring COC with low-dose spironolactone over metformin alone for hyperandrogenic manifestations, and metformin with low-dose spironolactone over either drug alone for symptom relief and adherence. It also describes evidence of greater weight loss and insulin sensitivity with GLP-1 agonists than with metformin.
clinical_implications: PCOS can occur without an elevated BMI, and apparently regular menstrual cycles do not necessarily establish normal ovulation.

Because PCOS shares manifestations with other disorders, its diagnosis requires consideration of alternative causes; acute onset or rapid progression of androgenic symptoms raises concern for an androgen-secreting tumor.

Adolescent diagnosis is particularly difficult because menstrual irregularity, acne and ovarian appearances can overlap with normal puberty; ultrasound and AMH have low diagnostic specificity in this group.

Associated reproductive, metabolic, sleep-related and mental health conditions contribute to the lifelong burden of PCOS. The increased risks described in the article should not be taken to mean that reduced longevity has been demonstrated.
Improvement in ovulation with age does not imply improved pregnancy or live-birth outcomes, which decline with age.
Endometrial exposure to estrogen without opposition may contribute to endometrial hyperplasia, and the article describes an increased risk of endometrial cancer in PCOS.
Excess weight can adversely affect pregnancy, miscarriage and live-birth outcomes following infertility treatment.
practice_implications: Diagnose PCOS in adults using 2 of the 3 stated criteria after excluding conditions with similar features. When irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism coexist, neither ovarian ultrasound nor AMH testing is needed; AMH alone must not establish the diagnosis.

Require both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction for an adolescent diagnosis; do not use ultrasound or AMH for diagnosis in adolescents. Where a presumptive diagnosis is treated with COCs, provide close follow-up and education pending diagnostic confirmation.

Assess menstrual and fertility history, clinical hyperandrogenism, adiposity and family history. Evaluate hirsutism objectively with the modified Ferriman-Gallwey score, using an ethnicity-dependent threshold of 4 to 6 while accounting for self-treatment.

If ovulation needs confirmation despite apparently regular cycles, measure serum progesterone. Consider thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia and atypical congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency; assess the latter with serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone and, when needed, an ACTH stimulation test.

Assess biochemical hyperandrogenism with total and free testosterone, estimating free testosterone through the calculated free androgen index when appropriate. If neither testosterone measure is elevated, consider androstenedione and DHEAS while recognizing their lower specificity.

Prefer LC-MS/MS over direct immunoassays for testosterone assessment. When androgen concentrations substantially exceed reference ranges, consider other causes; obtain the timing and rate of progression of symptoms because some androgen-secreting neoplasms produce only mild to moderate elevations.

For adult assessment of PCOM when imaging is needed, favor transvaginal ultrasound and FNPO; use an FNPO threshold of ≥20 in at least 1 ovary. AMH may help when an accurate ovarian ultrasound is unavailable, but must not serve as the sole diagnostic test.

Recommend lifestyle intervention for all women with PCOS, through exercise or combined dietary, exercise and behavioral approaches. Fertility is likely to return with a modest weight loss of about 5%, which can also improve manifestations.

For symptomatic menstrual irregularity, hirsutism or acne, use a combined hormonal contraceptive as first-line treatment after checking for contraindications. The article gives no preference among oral, patch and vaginal-ring delivery. For an oral contraceptive, it recommends an initial 20 µg of ethinyl estradiol with desogestrel, drospirenone or norethindrone acetate.

Consider spironolactone for hirsutism when response remains insufficient after at least 6 months of combined oral contraceptives or cosmetic treatment. Antiandrogen treatment requires reliable contraception because of teratogenic risk; consider adjunctive antiandrogens for moderate or severe hirsutism, or for mild hirsutism not adequately controlled after 6 months to 1 year of OCP.

Use cosmetic measures while waiting for pharmacologic treatment of hirsutism to take effect. The options described include bleaching, temporary hair removal, electrolysis for localized areas with an experienced operator, laser photo-epilation for generalized hirsutism and topical eflornithine for facial hirsutism, noting its potential serious adverse effects if absorbed systemically.

Metformin can be used for menstrual irregularity when hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated. Letrozole is presented as first-line treatment for infertility; for anovulatory infertility without other infertility factors, clomiphene citrate with metformin could be used instead of clomiphene citrate alone to improve ovulation and clinical pregnancy rates.

GLP1 has not been approved specifically for PCOS. The article encourages use of GLP1 for the named FDA-approved comorbid indications—OSA, Diabetes Mellitus, Obesity and heart failure—with individual monitoring of PCOS metabolic and phenotypic parameters. Use general-population guidance when considering bariatric/metabolic surgery.

Screen for ovulatory dysfunction and exclude other causes of infertility. Counsel women undergoing infertility treatment about the adverse effects of excess weight on clinical pregnancy, miscarriage and live-birth outcomes.
Do not routinely screen asymptomatic patients for endometrial thickness by ultrasound; advise reporting unexpected or abnormal uterine bleeding.

At diagnosis, assess BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, diabetes and lipids, with subsequent checks at a frequency guided by results. For IGT and type-2 diabetes mellitus screening, use an OGTT with fasting and 2-hour glucose after 75 g OGTT rather than relying on HbA1c, and repeat screening every 3 to 4 years.

Screen patients with overweight or obesity for OSA symptoms and refer for sleep studies when that screening is positive. Do not routinely measure LFT for MASLD unless the patient is overweight or obese.
Screen for depression and anxiety and provide appropriate treatment. Consider eating disorders and disordered eating regardless of weight, particularly during weight-management interventions.

When measuring testosterone, FSH, LH or AMH after COCs, consider testing only after the patient has been off COCs for at least 3 months. Acute or rapidly progressive adult hyperandrogenism should prompt consideration of adrenal or ovarian tumors.

Coordinate individualized care among relevant clinical, fertility, dermatologic, weight-management, mental health, pharmacy and nursing professionals. Use shared decision-making, patient education and support to align treatment with symptom, fertility and metabolic goals.
open_questions: The relative frequency of severe or minor adverse events with OCP alone, metformin alone and their combination remains uncertain, apart from the stated possibility of fewer severe and minor gastrointestinal adverse events with OCP alone than with the combination.
Fetal androgen exposure remains an etiologic hypothesis requiring validation.
future_directions: Conduct larger, well-designed RCTs stratified by BMI to assess metformin, OCPs and their combinations in women with PCOS, particularly adolescents.
Investigate newer GLP1s further for PCOS management.

notable_adverse_events: The review states that evidence is uncertain about differences in severe or minor adverse events between OCP alone, metformin alone, and metformin combined with OCP. It identifies an exception: OCP alone may result in fewer severe and minor gastrointestinal adverse events than OCP combined with metformin; no rates are reported.

Other antiandrogens, including cyproterone at doses over 10 mg per day, finasteride, flutamide, and bicalutamide, are described as carrying potential adverse-effect and toxicity risks; specific events and rates are not given.
Topical eflornithine for facial hirsutism is described as having potentially serious adverse effects if absorbed systemically; no event or rate is specified.
Myoinositol is described as causing fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects than metformin; no rates are supplied.

subgroup_analyses: Women diagnosed using NIH criteria had less hirsutism than those diagnosed using RC or RCAES criteria, according to cited prevalence research.
Women diagnosed using RC criteria had less prevalent IR than those diagnosed using NIH or RCAES criteria, according to cited research.
The cited evidence suggests PCOS prevalence is higher among Mexican Americans than among nonHispanic whites and African Americans.
Compared with controls matched on BMI, women with PCOS tended to have greater abdominal fat accumulation.
Cited evidence found elevated circulating C-reactive protein in individuals with PCOS compared with controls irrespective of obesity.
The review reports that metformin improves menstrual cycles, abnormal waist-to-hip ratio, and vascular markers in nonobese women with PCOS.
For adults with PCOS in the BMI 25 kg/m to 30 kg/m subgroup, metformin may be less effective than OCPs for hirsutism.
A cited 5-year follow-up study observed that some women initially classified as having classic PCOS (type A) no longer met PCOS criteria over time.
The review states that PCOS prevalence may be higher in Southeast Asian and Eastern Mediterranean regions despite being broadly similar across world regions.
secondary_results: The cited evidence links DENND1A to potential PCOS risk and identifies a role for microRNAs regulating GLUT4 in insulin resistance; fetal androgen exposure remains a hypothesis requiring validation.
A cited study identified impaired catecholamine sensitivity during lipolysis as an early indicator of insulin resistance.
In cited evidence, PCOS was associated with insulin resistance independently of adiposity.
The review reports that hirsutism and acne become less prevalent with age, while ovarian volume and follicle number decline; the age-related decline appears greater for follicle number.
Ovulation rates improve as women with PCOS age, but successful pregnancies and live births decrease with age, according to cited evidence.
The review reports an increased risk of endometrial cancer in PCOS, while noting that the two conditions share numerous risk factors.

Evidence cited by the review found more depressive symptoms, major depression, recurrent depression, and suicide attempts in women with PCOS; the depressive-symptom comparison used controls not matched on BMI.
The review estimates that around 70% of females with PCOS experience hirsutism and that around 70% of women with PCOS experience infertility.

document_sections.heading: Continuing Education Activity
document_sections.content: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is described as the most common endocrine disorder among females of reproductive age worldwide. Its pathophysiology chiefly involves insulin resistance and frequent visceral adiposity regardless of obesity, disrupting hormonal communication among the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and ovaries. Associated conditions include infertility, metabolic syndrome, obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risks, depression, obstructive sleep apnea, endometrial cancer, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Diagnosis depends on clinical criteria, but the condition has a multifactorial pathophysiology and poses diagnostic challenges. Delayed recognition can contribute to complications. Timely lifestyle measures are important for symptoms and quality of life, while long-term care requires an individualized focus on reproductive and metabolic health.

document_sections.heading: Objectives:
document_sections.content: The educational objectives are to recognize the importance of timely PCOS diagnosis, screen affected patients for comorbidities, provide appropriate management, and use interprofessional strategies to improve care coordination and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Stein and Leventhal first described PCOS in 1935. It is presented as the most common endocrine condition among females of reproductive age worldwide, with a prevalence between 5% and 26% depending on diagnostic criteria. Specialty guidelines generally require at least 2 of 3 features: chronic anovulation, clinical or biological hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries. Conditions with similar manifestations must be excluded. Diagnostic delay may allow comorbidities to progress and make lifestyle intervention harder to implement. Associated conditions include infertility, metabolic syndrome, obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular risk, depression, obstructive sleep apnea, endometrial cancer, and MASLD. Prevalence, phenotype, and pathogenic mechanisms vary across ethnic groups. Although PCOS is lifelong and metabolic, weight loss as low as 5% has been associated with a good response, including symptom resolution and better fertility outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Etiology
document_sections.content: PCOS is a complex multigenic condition with substantial epigenetic influences. Genome-wide association Studies (GWAS) have found several associated loci; implicated genes participate in insulin resistance, ovarian steroidogenesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, adrenal cortisone reductase deficiency, and gonadotrophic dysregulation. Twin research attributes about 70% of PCOS pathogenesis to genetic components. DENND1A (Differentially Expressed in Normal and Neoplastic Development isoform A1) has been proposed as a risk marker. Obesity can promote hypermethylation in ovarian granulosa cells and suppress gene expression. Fetal androgen exposure remains a hypothesis requiring validation. A regulatory role for microRNAs affecting GLUT4 in insulin resistance has also been validated.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: PCOS affects between 5% and 26% of females of reproductive age worldwide and is increasingly recognized as their most common endocrine condition. Rotterdam criteria (RC), commonly used in prevalence studies, are broader than the National Institute of Health 1990 Criteria. The Revised Rotterdam Criteria by Androgen Excess Society (RCAES) are more sensitive than RC for a phenotype combining polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) and infertility. Women diagnosed with NIH criteria had less hirsutism than those diagnosed with RC or RCAES; the RC group had less insulin resistance (IR) than the NIH and RCAES groups. Conversely, more than 80% of women presenting with hyperandrogenism have PCOS. The NIH 2012 workshop report estimated about 5 million affected females of reproductive age in the United States and approximately 4 billion annually in healthcare costs for diagnosis and treatment, excluding severe associated comorbidities. Associated conditions include infertility, metabolic syndrome, obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular risk, depression, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), endometrial cancer, and MASLD. Higher prevalence has been linked to first-degree relatives with PCOS, prepubertal obesity, congenital virilizing disorders, aboveaverage or low birth weight for gestational age, premature adrenarche, and use of valproic acid as an antiepileptic drug. Studies suggest greater prevalence among Mexican Americans than among nonHispanic whites or African Americans. Geographic variation in diagnostic features and overall heterogeneity warrant consideration. In a 5-year follow-up study, some women initially classified with classic PCOS (type A) no longer met PCOS criteria over time.

document_sections.heading: Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: PCOS has interacting abnormalities in ovarian steroidogenesis, insulin resistance, antimullerian hormone (AMH), and excess Luteinizing hormone (LH) arising from hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis dysfunction. Recent literature increasingly treats it as a metabolic disease. Hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess reinforce one another. Insulin resistance produces hyperinsulinemia in 70% of females with PCOS; reduced catecholamine responsiveness during lipolysis has been demonstrated as an early insulin-resistance indicator. Insulin increases ovarian sensitivity to LH by disrupting normal homologous LH desensitization and intraovarian regulatory balance. Insulin-like growth factors (IGF) interact with FSH in GC cells to affect follicle maturation and steroid production. PCOS theca cells overexpress many androgen-synthesis enzymes and proteins, including P450c17, suggesting a prominent steroidogenic abnormality. Excess androgen and insulin promote early luteinization of granulosa cells. Hyperinsulinemia also affects hepatic IGF1 binding protein and SHBG and the adrenal steroid response to hyperandrogenemia. FSH and IGF1 in GC form a positive feedback process needed for follicular dominance and maturation; altered IGF1 during hyperinsulinemia can impair maturation and cause oligo-ovulation, while androgen excess further disrupts IGF1. PCOS-associated insulin resistance does not depend on adiposity. Compared with controls, affected individuals have higher circulating C-reactive protein regardless of obesity, consistent with chronic low-grade inflammation. Two-thirds of presentations have typical functional ovarian hyperandrogenism, with excessive 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) response to gonadotropin stimulation. The remaining 20% to 30% show an atypical FOH 17-OHP response, although testosterone elevation can be identified after adrenal androgen suppression. About 3% have associated isolated functional adrenal hyperandrogenism. Specific FOH-subpopulation testing currently has little clinical utility. Excess androgen increases primordial-follicle recruitment but also causes premature luteinization and interferes with dominant-follicle selection, producing the anatomical and histopathological changes of PCOM. LH excess is frequent and supports gonadal steroidogenic enzymes and sex-hormone secretion, but LH-induced theca-cell desensitization makes it less likely to initiate ovarian androgen excess. Hyperandrogenemia can increase LH, sustaining a cycle involving theca and luteinized granulosa cells. Waist-to-height ratio correlates more strongly with hyperandrogenism than other anthropometric measures. Ovarian hormonal dysregulation changes pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone release and may increase LH relative to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). LH stimulates ovarian androgen formation, whereas relatively lower FSH reduces granulosa-cell aromatase stimulation and conversion of androgens to estradiol. The resulting hormonal pattern persists without normal cycling. Peripheral tissues convert elevated circulating androgens mainly to estrone; adipose stromal cells mediate much of this conversion, increasing estrogen production in obese patients. Sustained estrogen feedback differs from the normal fluctuations accompanying follicular growth, and estrogen stimulation without opposition may cause endometrial hyperplasia. Animal studies have recently implicated autoimmune responses and chronic inflammation in abnormal follicular development and fertility outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Histopathology
document_sections.content: Rat models of PCOS have shown multiple follicular cysts with thin, degenerating granulosa-cell layers.

document_sections.heading: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Clinical Features
document_sections.content: A comprehensive clinical assessment is essential because history and examination inform 2 out of 3 diagnostic criteria and help identify alternative conditions. Relevant information includes menstrual and fertility history, obesity, and hyperandrogenic features. Under the 2023 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guidelines, irregular cycles are characterized as follows: cycles in the first year postmenarche are considered part of normal pubertal transition; within 1 to <3 years postmenarche, intervals <21 or >45 days are irregular; from 3 years postmenarche until perimenopause, intervals <21 or >35 days or <8 cycles per year are irregular; any cycle 1 year postmenarche with an interval >90 days is irregular; and primary amenorrhea by age 15 or >3 years post thelarche (breast development) is included. Hair loss may affect the vertex or crown or be diffuse; more severe hyperandrogenism may cause bitemporal loss and frontal hairline recession. Adolescents with severe acne or acne resistant to oral or topical antibiotics may have a 40% chance of developing PCOS. Persistent or worsening acne in females in their mid-20s to 30s calls for particular attention to hyperandrogenism. Hirsutism consists of coarse, dark terminal hair in a typically male distribution. Increased muscle mass, reduced breast size, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly are uncommon in PCOS; such virilization suggests elevated androgens and warrants investigation, especially for an ovarian or adrenal androgen-producing tumor. Hirsutism should be assessed objectively with the modified Ferrim-Gallwey scoring system. Depending on ethnicity, a modified Ferriman-Gallwey score (mFG) of 4 to 6 should be used for detection, while recognizing that self-treatment can obscure examination findings.

document_sections.heading: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Risk Factors and Phenotypes
document_sections.content: Assessment should account for a family history of PCOS or metabolic syndrome and possible fetal androgen exposure. Although 38% to 88% of women with PCOS are overweight or obese, they tend to accumulate more abdominal fat than body mass index (BMI)-matched controls; normal BMI therefore does not rule out PCOS. The Androgen Excess Society cautions that apparently regular menses can coexist with oligo-ovulation. In patients with clinical hyperandrogenism and apparent eumenorrhea, progesterone measurement should be used to assess ovulatory function further. A PCOS task force described 7 phenotypes (A to G) using hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, oligo-anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. The most common, phenotype A or the classic phenotype, has all 4 features: hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, oligo/anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. Phenotypes tend to improve with age, alongside reduced hyperandrogenism and increased FSH.

document_sections.heading: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Diagnostic Criteria
document_sections.content: Most society guidelines accept a PCOS diagnosis when 2 out of 3 Rotterdam Criteria are present—chronic oligo-anovulation, clinical or biological hyperandrogenism, and PCOM—and other pathology has been excluded. National Institute of Health criteria require both clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism and oligo or anovulation; Rotterdam Criteria are used most often. For adults, the International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023 requires 2 out of 3 findings—clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound or elevated AMH—plus exclusion of similar diagnoses. Adults with both irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism need neither ultrasound nor AMH measurement for diagnosis. Adolescents require both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction; ultrasound and AMH are not recommended for them because specificity is low. A history of irregular cycles can establish chronic oligo-ovulation or anovulation. Regular cycles do not exclude ovulatory dysfunction, and serum progesterone can be measured when confirmation of anovulation is needed. Thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, and atypical congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency should be excluded. Evaluation for the last condition requires serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone and may require a subsequent adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test.

document_sections.heading: Hyperandrogenism Diagnostic Evaluation
document_sections.content: In adult women, hirsutism, alopecia, and acne indicate clinical hyperandrogenism and can signal biochemical hyperandrogenism. Assessment should measure total and free testosterone; the calculated free androgen index can estimate free testosterone. If neither measure is elevated, androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) may be considered, recognizing their lower specificity and the tendency of DHEA to decline with age. Laboratories should favor LC-MS/MS assays rather than direct immunoassays, including radiometric or enzyme-linked methods, for total or free testosterone because direct assays have limited accuracy, sensitivity, and precision in this setting. Androgen concentrations substantially above laboratory reference ranges should prompt consideration of ovarian or adrenal neoplasms, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis—particularly after menopause—iatrogenic effects, and severe-insulin-resistance syndromes. Some androgen-secreting neoplasms cause only mild or moderate elevations, so the timing of onset and speed of progression are important clinical-history details.

document_sections.heading: Imaging Findings of Polycystic Ovaries
document_sections.content: Transvaginal ultrasound provides a more accurate assessment of ovarian morphology. In adults, follicles per ovary (FNPO) is the most effective ultrasound marker of PCOM; follicles per cross-section (FNPS) and ovarian volume (OV) are also reliable. The adult PCOM threshold is FNPO ≥20 in at least 1 ovary. Ultrasound is unnecessary for PCOS diagnosis when irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism coexist. AMH may help establish the diagnosis when accurate ultrasound assessment of PCOM is unavailable, but AMH cannot diagnose PCOS on its own and should not be used diagnostically in adolescents.

document_sections.heading: Lifestyle Modification
document_sections.content: Lifestyle change is presented as the primary and most effective approach to PCOS management. Modest weight loss of about 5% is likely to restore fertility and can be achieved with a low-calorie diet, which also improves ovarian structure. Exercise alone or combined dietary, exercise, and behavioral interventions should be recommended to all women with PCOS to reduce metabolic dysfunction. Reductions in central adiposity and normalization of the lipid profile can be used to monitor metabolic improvement.

document_sections.heading: Hormonal contraceptives
document_sections.content: A combined hormonal contraceptive is first-line treatment for symptomatic menstrual irregularity, hirsutism, and acne in PCOS. Oral contraceptive (COC), patch, and vaginal-ring delivery are options; the Endocrine Society does not favor one method. The progestin component lowers LH and consequently ovarian androgen production while increasing sex hormone-binding globulin. Some progestins also directly inhibit 5 alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of free testosterone into 5 alpha-dihydrotestosterone. These actions support menstrual regulation and control of hyperandrogenic symptoms. Contraindications must be identified before treatment. Higher estrogen levels tend to raise high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol and lower low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. No significant difference in body weight or fat distribution has been demonstrated between women with and without PCOS. For oral contraception, the recommended initial regimen is 20 µg of ethinyl estradiol with an antiandrogenic progestin such as desogestrel or drospirenone, or a neutral progestin such as norethindrone acetate. Studies found COC plus low-dose spironolactone more effective than metformin alone for reducing hyperandrogenic symptoms and biochemical markers. Other findings suggest that metformin plus low-dose spironolactone improves symptoms and medication adherence more than either drug alone. spironolactone may be considered for hirsutism if response remains inadequate after at least 6 months of combined oral contraceptives or cosmetic treatment. cyproterone (at doses over 10 mg per day), finasteride, flutamide, and bicalutamide carry potential adverse-effect and toxicity risks.

document_sections.heading: Metformin
document_sections.content: As PCOS is increasingly viewed as a metabolic condition, metformin and other insulin sensitizers have attracted therapeutic interest. In nonobese women with PCOS, metformin improves menstrual cycles, an abnormal waist-to-hip ratio, and vascular markers. In adult women in the subgroup BMI 25 kg/m to 30 kg/m, metformin may improve hirsutism less effectively than OCPs; either treatment alone may be less effective than their combination. Differences in severe or minor adverse events between either treatment alone and the combination remain uncertain, except that OCP alone may reduce severe and minor gastrointestinal adverse events relative to OCP plus metformin. Larger, well-designed RCTs stratified by BMI are needed, particularly for adolescents. metformin can be used for menstrual irregularity when hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated. Commonly used alone in adolescents, it helps restore normal menses, promotes weight loss, reduces insulin resistance, and may mildly improve androgen-excess symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Infertility Treatment
document_sections.content: letrozole is first-line treatment for infertility associated with PCOS. For women with anovulatory infertility and no other infertility factors, clomiphene citrate plus metformin could be used instead of clomiphene citrate alone to improve ovulation and clinical pregnancy rates.

document_sections.heading: Symptom-based Treatment for Hirsutism, Alopecia, and Acne
document_sections.content: Clinical hyperandrogenism requires prolonged treatment, with effects becoming apparent only after several months. Cosmetic measures should begin while medication takes effect. Options include bleaching, temporary hair removal, galvanic or blended electrolysis performed by an experienced operator for localized areas, and laser photo-epilation for generalized hirsutism. Topical eflornithine can treat facial hirsutism, but it may be costly and can have potentially serious adverse effects if systemically absorbed. Low-dose neutral or antiandrogenic oral contraceptives are first-line treatment for hirsutism and lower androgen levels and effects. Their contraceptive action is also useful alongside antiandrogens, which are highly teratogenic and require reliable contraception. OCP alone can treat mild hirsutism. Adjunct antiandrogens can be considered for moderate or severe hirsutism, or for mild hirsutism inadequately controlled after 6 months to 1 year of OCP.

document_sections.heading: Additional Insulin Sensitizing Treatment in PCOS GLP-1 agonists
document_sections.content: In obese women with PCOS, treatment with GLP-1 agonists has been associated with lower BMI and testosterone and a higher ovulation rate. Growing evidence suggests greater weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity with GLP-1 agonists than with metformin. GLP1 has not been approved specifically to manage PCOS. A 2-year observational study assessed long-term weight maintenance after 16-week semaglutide treatment followed by continued metformin; it reported net weight loss and lower circulating testosterone during semaglutide use. Newer GLP1s require further study for PCOS management. The article encourages using GLP1 for co-morbid FDA-approved indications such as OSA, Diabetes Mellitus, Obesity, and heart failure, with individual monitoring of metabolic and phenotypic PCOS changes.

document_sections.heading: Myoinositol
document_sections.content: Myoinositol is an over-the-counter supplement that increases insulin sensitivity. Compared with placebo, it improved insulin sensitivity in women with PCOS without significantly changing BMI. Evidence remains limited. Its use has mainly involved PCOS fertility treatment or situations in which metformin is not tolerated, because it causes fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects.

document_sections.heading: Bariatric surgery
document_sections.content: Decisions about bariatric/metabolic surgery for women with PCOS should follow guidelines for the general population.

document_sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Conditions and exposures considered in the differential diagnosis are use of androgenic steroids, hypothyroidism, late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia, idiopathic/familial hirsutism, and ovarian malignancies.

document_sections.heading: Prognosis
document_sections.content: Hirsutism and acne become less prevalent with age. Ovarian volume and follicle count also decline, with follicle count apparently falling more than ovarian volume. Ovulation rates improve as women with PCOS age, but successful pregnancies and live births become less frequent. Reported outcomes include a 41% to 64.8% pregnancy success rate among females treated with letrozole, a cumulative live-birth rate of 31% (average 3 attempts) with intrauterine insemination (IUI), and a 29% liver-birth rate after in-vitro fertilization (IVF). In a population-based retrospective reproductive-age cohort from Western Australia, women with PCOS had more nonobstetric, noninjury hospital admissions than the general population (median, 5 versus 2; P < .001). The PCOS and comparison groups, respectively, had reported rates of adult-onset diabetes of 12.5 versus 3.8%, obesity of 16.0 versus 3.7%, hypertensive disorder of 3.8 versus 0.7%, ischemic heart disease of 0.8 versus 0.2%, cerebrovascular disease of 0.6 versus 0.2%, arterial and venous disease of 0.5 versus 0.2% and 10.4 versus 5.6%, respectively, asthma of 10.6 vs 4.5%, stress/anxiety of 14.0 vs 5.9%, depression of 9.8 versus 4.3%, licit/illicit drug-related admissions of 8.8 versus 4.5%, self-harm of 7.2 versus 2.9%, land transport accidents of 5.2 versus 3.8%, and mortality of 0.7 versus 0.4% (all P < .001). Women with PCOS also had higher admission rates for menorrhagia (14.1 versus 3.6%), infertility treatment (40.9 versus 4.6%), and miscarriage (11.1 versus 6.1%), and more often required in vitro fertilization (17.2 versus 2.0%). Despite these elevated risks, a separate 32-year prospective study assessing women with PCOS at ages 72-91 found no evidence of increased all-cause or cardiovascular mortality.

document_sections.heading: Infertility
document_sections.content: Endocrine Society Guidelines recommend assessing ovulatory status in every patient. Eumenorrheic cycles can still be anovulatory; mid-luteal serum progesterone can assess this. Other causes of infertility should also be excluded.

document_sections.heading: Obstetric Complications
document_sections.content: Women with PCOS should receive counseling about the adverse effects of excess weight on clinical pregnancy, miscarriage, and live-birth rates after infertility treatment.

document_sections.heading: Endometrial Cancer
document_sections.content: Multiple studies report increased endometrial-cancer risk in PCOS, and the conditions share numerous risk factors. The Endocrine Society advises against routine ultrasound (US) screening of endometrial thickness in asymptomatic patients. Women should instead be advised to report unexpected or abnormal uterine bleeding.

document_sections.heading: Metabolic and Cardiovascular Diseases
document_sections.content: Women and adolescents with PCOS should be screened for obesity using BMI and waist circumference. Blood pressure, diabetes, and lipids should be assessed at diagnosis, with subsequent testing frequency determined by the findings. Approximately 33% to 66% of patients have an abnormal degree of insulin resistance. Endocrine Society guidelines recommend an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), including fasting glucose and 2-hour glucose after a 75 g OGTT, to screen for IGT and type-2 diabetes mellitus. OGTT is preferred to HbA1c because HbA1c has lower sensitivity in PCOS. Repeat screening is advised every 3 to 4 years because risk factors occur more often than in the general population. Patients with overweight or obesity should also be screened for OSA symptoms and referred for sleep studies when screening is positive.

document_sections.heading: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease
document_sections.content: Women with PCOS have 3 times the risk of MASLD, formerly termed nonalcoholic fatty liver disease NAFLD. MASLD has been associated with androgen excess and low sex hormone-binding globulin. Routine LFT measurement is not recommended unless the patient has overweight or obesity, given its low sensitivity and specificity for MASLD diagnosis. In such patients, changing management to newer antidiabetic medications such as GLP-1 agonists can reduce the risk of developing NAFLD.

document_sections.heading: Depression
document_sections.content: Women with PCOS have shown higher rates of depressive symptoms than controls not matched for BMI. Major depression, recurrent depression, and suicide attempts were also more frequent. Depression and anxiety disorders should be screened for and identified, followed by appropriate treatment.

document_sections.heading: Deterrence and Patient Education
document_sections.content: PCOS encompasses manifestations in multiple body systems. Increased male-hormone activity may appear as hirsutism, hair loss, or acne, or be identified through hormone testing; irregular cycles and infertility may also occur. Diagnosis requires consideration of symptoms, examination, laboratory findings, and imaging rather than any single test that confirms or excludes PCOS. Familial occurrence reflects interactions among multiple genes rather than just 1 gene. In certain ethnicities, prevalence is estimated at 1 in 4 women aged 18 to 35 years. Insulin resistance is implicated in initiating and maintaining the hormonal disturbance and is also central to diabetes and obesity. The proposed treatment approach emphasizes at least 5% weight loss, even for lean females with PCOS, with a good response; options discussed include metformin and injectable weight-loss/diabetes medications, tailored to individual goals. Around 70% of affected females experience hirsutism, which may be managed with hormonal pills and hair-removal approaches such as laser, electrolysis, or shaving. Around 70% experience infertility. A 5% weight loss has been reported to restore fertility; if unsuccessful, metformin and specialist infertility treatment are recommended. Across the lifespan, affected females face higher risks of infertility, high-risk pregnancy, miscarriage, diabetes, sleep apnea, obesity, endometrial cancer, depression, and heart disease, although an effect on longevity has not been shown. The daily and long-term burden has psychological and economic consequences. Peer support, engagement with healthcare teams, patient self-advocacy, and broader awareness may help address stigma.

document_sections.heading: Pearls and Other Issues
document_sections.content: Adolescent diagnosis is difficult because acne, menstrual irregularity, and hyperinsulinemia can accompany normal puberty. Immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis can cause irregular anovulatory cycles during the first 2 to 3 years after menarche. Oligomenorrhea persisting beyond that period predicts continued irregular cycles and a greater likelihood of ovarian or adrenal dysfunction. Ultrasound has limited value in adolescents because large multicystic ovaries are common. COCs may be started for a presumptive diagnosis, with close follow-up and education while definitive confirmation is deferred. Testosterone, FSH, LH, and AMH cannot be measured reliably during COC use; clinicians should consider measurement after at least 3 months off COCs. New or rapidly progressive adult hyperandrogenism should prompt consideration of adrenal or ovarian tumors. PCOS prevalence is broadly similar across regions but may be higher in Southeast Asian and Eastern Mediterranean regions. Eating disorders and disordered eating should be considered regardless of weight, particularly during weight management and lifestyle intervention.

document_sections.heading: Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
document_sections.content: PCOS management calls for coordinated, patient-centered care across professions. Physicians and advanced practitioners diagnose, begin treatment, and coordinate services. Dermatologists manage hirsutism and acne; reproductive endocrinologists and infertility specialists address ovulatory dysfunction and fertility; obesity medicine practitioners and registered dietitians individualize weight-management and lifestyle strategies. Psychiatrists and counselors address depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. Pharmacists support safe use of hormonal contraceptives, insulin sensitizers, and antiandrogens, including counseling about adherence and adverse effects. Communication and coordination among professionals are important for outcomes, safety, and team performance. Nurses educate patients and facilitate follow-up. Medical estheticians and patient advocates can address cosmetic concerns and stigma. Education should also reach fitness trainers and estheticians, who may first notice hirsutism or unexplained weight gain. Shared decision-making can align symptom, fertility, and metabolic-risk management with patient goals. Support groups may improve well-being and reduce stress. Collaborative care is presented as a way to support earlier recognition, timely treatment, and better quality of life.
